growth.note: The growth tool's inputs (tools/grow_species.mjs,     docs/tree-architecture.md): the tree grown through its life by its limb mechanics and the generator's age classes fitted to it. Each value with its source and the date it was read.

height_m_by_age.source: Chapman-Richards fit (2026-11-01) to the 49 aged Sacramento valley oaks of the Urban Tree Database (McPherson,     van Doorn and Peper 2016,     RDS-2016-0005,     TS3): 9.4 m at 10 y,     16.6 at 30,     20.6 at 80,     21 at 200; the raw 100-220-year trees stand 20-31 m and the fit's own asymptote is 19.5; held at 21 for FEIS's usual 15-25 m. Urban,     irrigated trees grow fast

dbh_cm_by_age.source: the same fit: 18 cm at 10 y,     42 at 30,     81 at 80,     130 at 200,     148 at 300 (the database's cubic,     rounded,     turns over past 150 y)

crown_width_m_by_dbh_cm.source: Bechtold 2004 table 3 (equation 3,     stand-grown largest crown width,     valley oak n 29,     dbh 5-47 in): LCW ft = 2.9954 + 1.9137 dbh in,     in metres per cm; a check,     not an input. The Urban Tree Database's crown diameter by age: 6.3 m at 10 y,     12.6 at 30,     18.7 at 80,     21 at 200 (fit 2026-11-01),     W/H 0.56 under 6 y,     0.74 at 6-20,     0.91 at 20-40,     0.94 at 40-90,     1.14 past 160

crown_width_m_by_age.source: Chapman-Richards fit (2026-11-01) to the Urban Tree Database's crown diameters by age (the 49 aged Sacramento trees): 6.3 m at 10 y,     12.6 at 30,     18.7 at 80,     21 at 200; drives the laterals' extension

wood.source: green density about 1,    000 (van Rooij et al. 2023 take green wood as water; the Wood Handbook's green white oak about 990); modulus: white oak green,     Wood Handbook FPL-GTR-190 table 5-3a,     no value exists for Q. lobata (green oaks 6-11 GPa); dry density 550 from the Urban Tree Database's volume-to-biomass table (Pillsbury,     Reimer and Thompson 1998),     2026-11-01
wood.modulus_effective_note: tuned 2026-11-01 against the photographs (docs/tree-likeness-review.md,     the record's targets.photos): at the Wood Handbook's green modulus over a creep factor of 2 (4.3 GPa) the grown limbs stay level to 200 y; at 2.5 the sag is heavy by 80 y and the ends barely rise; 2.8 gives a mature tree with level scaffolds whose ends rise and a veteran whose limbs arch below horizontal with the ends turned up. Branch wood is juvenile wood with knots (50-70 % of the clear-specimen modulus) under decades of creep; MAppleT fitted 1.1 GPa for apple limbs (1-7 tested). The trunk is stiffened 3 x: the loop has no eccentric growth or whole-tree righting,     which hold a real trunk upright

leaf.source: leaf area: Urban Tree Database TS6,     SacVal QULO,     loglogw1 exp(a + b ln ln(dbh + 1) + mse/2),     dbh 2-135 cm (880 m2 at 80 cm); leaf mass: 115 g/m2 dry,     the median of the database's deciduous oaks in TS5 (laurel 118-136,     Shumard 110,     red 109,     water 148; no valley oak sample),     over dw/fw 0.48; the load per shoot is the total over the live tips

description: The biggest oak in California: 15-30 m tall,     with a massive grey trunk,     a broad dome of long limbs whose outer branches droop toward the ground,     and deeply lobed leaves with rounded lobes. It grows on deep soils of the valley floors and lower slopes,     where its roots reach the water table,     and its long acorns feed deer,     squirrels,     jays,     woodpeckers and wild turkeys.

season_notes.winter: Bare: the great grey limbs and the hanging tips of the outer branches show,     with green balls of mistletoe high in the crown.
season_notes.spring: Leaves come out pale green in March with hanging catkins; this year's acorns start on the new shoots.
season_notes.summer: In full dark green leaf,     the deepest shade in the valley; the long acorns grow through the summer.
season_notes.fall: The long acorns ripen and drop (September-November) and the leaves turn yellow-brown before falling.

riparian.water: Its deep roots reach the water table under valley floors and creek terraces; it needs no surface water and stands well back from the channel on deep soil.

roots.note: wide-spreading laterals over a deep sinker system

notes: Valley oak is the largest North American oak: usually 10-25 m (FEIS),     here 15-25 m in the file with a veteran class to 30 m,     dbh 0.5-0.7 m commonly and well over 1.5 m on old trees (radius_ratio 0.06; veterans 1.35x). Long-lived (300-500+ years). It needs deep alluvial soil with groundwater in reach,     so around Placerville and Shingle Springs it stands on valley floors,     swales and the lower slopes,     mostly below about 600 m,     with blue oak on the drier slopes above. Decurrent Rauh's model like the other oaks: a short,     massive trunk (trunk.length_ratio 0.32) forking into a few heavy scaffold limbs (split_prob 0.5) that spread wide and arch down (level-1 droop_deg 28),     with long pendulous outer branchlets (level-2 tropism -0.06,     droop_deg 16): the drooping skirt that sets valley oak apart from blue oak at a glance,     strongest in veterans (droop_deg 40). Open-grown crowns in the photographs are 1.3-1.8 times as wide as tall with the crown base at 0.06-0.12 of the height. Bark grey,     thick,     deeply furrowed into small rectangular blocks ('platy' with small plates,     8-14 cm; it is checkered more coarsely and darker than blue oak's). Leaves 5-10 cm,     deeply cut into 7-11 rounded lobes,     dark green above and paler,     finely hairy below: leaf_shape lobed_large (2026-10-26,     was oblong_wavy,     which does not read lobe_depth) with 9 round-tipped pinnate lobes cut 0.55 of the way in (lobes,     lobe_depth,     lobe_tip round,     lobe_style pinnate) at leaf_size_m 0.08,     and a paler palette tint for the undersides. Deciduous: leafs out in March,     holds its leaves into November or December,     yellow-brown in fall (leaf_on.fall 0.75),     bare in winter with fine pendulous twigs (winter_twigs). Oak mistletoe (Phoradendron) is common in valley oak crowns (mistletoe prob 0.5,     veterans 0.8). Acorns: yes,     for the acorn game. Long and slender (3-5 cm),     ripening in one season and dropping September-November; scrub-jays and ground squirrels cache them.
